# PoolChem Tracker

> A free iOS app for tracking pool water chemistry. No account, no cloud, no ads — all data stays on your device.

PoolChem Tracker helps residential pool owners monitor and balance their water chemistry. Log readings for Free Chlorine, Total Chlorine, pH, Total Alkalinity, Calcium Hardness, Cyanuric Acid, Salt, and Water Temperature. The app calculates your Langelier Saturation Index (LSI), generates a health score, and gives plain-language dosing recommendations based on your pool size.

## Key Facts

- Platform: iOS, Android
- Pricing: Free with optional Pro upgrade (one-time purchase)
- Ads: None
- Account required: No
- Cloud sync: No
- Data storage: On-device only
- Internet connection: Not required for logging chemistry

## Blog

- [What Chemicals Do I Need for a Pool](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/blog/what-chemicals-do-i-need-for-a-pool): Essential pool chemicals, what each does, and what to skip
- [Pool Chemistry for Beginners](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/blog/pool-chemistry-beginners): The 5 numbers every pool owner should know — FC, pH, TA, CH, CYA — with target ranges and why each matters
- [How to Balance Pool Water](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/blog/how-to-balance-pool-water): 4-step order — alkalinity first, then pH, then calcium, then chlorine — and why doing it out of order wastes chemicals
- [How to Raise Pool Chlorine](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/blog/how-to-raise-pool-chlorine): Liquid chlorine vs cal-hypo vs tablets, dose math by pool size, and why CYA changes the target you need to hit
- [How to Lower Pool Alkalinity](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/blog/how-to-lower-pool-alkalinity): Muriatic acid method to drop TA without crashing pH; includes aeration step and how much acid to add
- [How to Raise Pool Alkalinity](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/blog/how-to-raise-pool-alkalinity): Baking soda raises TA ~10 ppm per 1.5 lbs per 10k gallons; raise TA first when both TA and pH are low; dose reference table by pool size and current TA
- [Pool Chlorine Too Low](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/blog/pool-chlorine-too-low): Why chlorine reads zero or near zero — usually low CYA, high demand from organics, or under-dosing — and how to recover
- [Pool pH Too High](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/blog/pool-ph-too-high): Causes (high TA, fresh plaster, aeration) and fixes — muriatic acid dosing chart and how to keep pH from rebounding
- [Pool pH Too Low](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/blog/pool-ph-too-low): pH below 7.2 means corrosive water; soda ash raises pH quickly when TA is in range, baking soda when both TA and pH are low — includes dose reference table and product decision guide
- [Why Is My Pool Water Cloudy? 5 Causes + Diagnosis Chart](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/blog/why-is-my-pool-water-cloudy): Pillar guide — 5 causes of cloudy or hazy pool water (low FC, high pH, high TA, high calcium causing white/milky water, poor filtration); diagnostic ladder with fix order, clarifier vs flocculant, cloudy after adding chemicals (shock, baking soda, algaecide, calcium increaser), spring opening, and after-rain scenarios
- [Pool Water Green but Chlorine Is High](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/blog/pool-water-green-but-chlorine-is-high): Usually metals (copper/iron) rather than algae — how to tell the difference and use sequestrant to clear it
- [Best Time to Test Pool Water: Morning (Before 10 AM)](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/blog/best-time-to-test-pool-water): Test before 10 AM — UV destroys FC throughout the day; test 2–3× per week in swim season, after shocking, and any time you add chemicals
- [How Often to Test Pool Water](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/blog/how-often-to-test-pool-water): FC/pH 2–3x per week, TA/CH weekly, CYA monthly — adjusted for SWG, heavy use, and after rain
- [What Is CYA (Pool Stabilizer)?](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/blog/cya-pool-stabilizer): Cyanuric acid protects chlorine from UV breakdown but raises required FC; ideal 30–50 ppm for regular pools, 60–80 ppm for SWG; minimum FC = CYA × 7.5% (×5% for SWG); only drain/refill lowers CYA; covers sources (trichlor tablets add CYA; liquid chlorine and cal-hypo do not), how to raise and lower, and effects on LSI
- [How to Lower CYA in a Pool](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/blog/how-to-lower-cya): Only dilution works — drain fraction = (current CYA − target CYA) / current CYA; e.g. CYA 80 → target 40 requires 50% drain; no chemical reliably removes CYA; hard fill water warning (high CH fill water can raise CH while lowering CYA); rebalance TA, pH, CH, FC after refill; switch to liquid chlorine after to prevent recurrence
- [How to Raise CYA in a Pool](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/blog/how-to-raise-cya): Add granular cyanuric acid (pool stabilizer/conditioner); ~13 oz per 10,000 gal raises CYA 10 ppm; pre-dissolve in warm water or sock near return jet — never add to skimmer basket; wait 24–48h before retesting; target 30–50 ppm regular, 60–80 ppm SWG; trichlor tablets also raise CYA at season startup but switch to liquid chlorine once at target
- [How Much Stabilizer to Add to a Pool](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/blog/how-much-stabilizer-to-add): Formula: oz = (target ppm increase × pool gallons) ÷ 7,500; ~13 oz per 10K gal = +10 ppm; dose chart for 10K–30K gal pools in +10/+20/+30/+40 ppm increments; pre-dissolve in bucket of warm water, pour near return jet, never into skimmer basket; wait 24–48h before retesting; liquid chlorine pools add once at season start then small top-ups; trichlor pools usually don't need it (tablets add CYA continuously)
- [Low CYA in a Pool: Signs, Risks, and How to Fix It](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/blog/low-cya-in-pool): CYA below 20 ppm leaves chlorine unprotected from UV; at CYA 0 unstabilized FC has a ~35-min half-life in direct sunlight, most FC lost in 4–6 hours; signs are daytime chlorine loss pattern, algae after any dosing gap, high chlorine consumption; caused by fresh fill, over-draining, dilution from rain, or switching from trichlor to liquid chlorine; fix is granular stabilizer to reach 30–50 ppm; indoor pools intentionally keep CYA near zero (no UV benefit)
- [Best CYA Level for Liquid Chlorine Pools](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/blog/best-cya-level-for-liquid-chlorine): Ideal CYA is 30–50 ppm (40 ppm sweet spot) for sodium hypochlorite pools; below 30 ppm UV destroys FC too fast, above 60–70 ppm FC minimum rises past what most owners maintain; liquid chlorine adds zero CYA so once in range it stays stable; raise with granular stabilizer (13 oz per 10K gal = +10 ppm); trichlor tablets acceptable at season startup to reach target but switch to liquid chlorine after
- [High CYA in a Pool: Symptoms, Causes, and How to Fix It](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/blog/high-cya-in-pool): CYA above 80 ppm raises required FC minimum (CYA × 7.5%) to levels most pool owners don't maintain — chronic under-sanitization follows; symptoms include recurring algae despite positive chlorine test, shock that doesn't hold, and chlorine burning through fast; primary cause is trichlor tablets as main chlorine source; fix is partial drain (drain fraction = (current − target) / current); no chemical reliably removes CYA
- [FC/CYA Chart: 5–7 ppm at CYA 50, 7–9 ppm at CYA 80](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/blog/fc-cya-chart-chlorine-levels): Minimum FC = CYA × 7.5%; full chart with minimum, target, and shock FC at every CYA value from 0–100 ppm
- [Pool Chlorine Levels Chart](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/blog/pool-chlorine-levels-chart): FC, TC, and CC explained — what each means, safe ranges, chloramine formation, and when to act
- [Pool Chemistry Cheat Sheet](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/blog/pool-chemistry-cheat-sheet): One-page reference for all pool chemistry ranges
- [Why LSI Matters](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/blog/what-is-lsi): What corrosive and scale-forming water actually does to pool surfaces and equipment — plaster etching, heat exchanger fouling, salt cell damage — and how to catch it before the repair bills arrive
- [Why Two LSI Calculators Disagree](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/blog/why-lsi-calculators-disagree): The four formula differences that cause different LSI results — CYA alkalinity correction, temperature factor method, TDS inclusion, and factor table rounding — with a concrete worked comparison
- [CSI vs. LSI](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/blog/csi-vs-lsi): CSI (Calcite Saturation Index) and LSI (Langelier Saturation Index) measure the same thing with nearly identical formulas — the name doesn't determine accuracy, the formula implementation does (CYA correction, TDS inclusion)
- [LSI by Pool Surface Type](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/blog/lsi-pool-surface-types): How LSI consequences differ for plaster (dissolves surface directly), vinyl (liner safe but metal walls corrode), and fiberglass (gel coat safe but scale nearly impossible to remove) — with CH targets and practical bias for each surface type
- [Why Your LSI Changes After It Rains](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/blog/why-lsi-changes-after-rain): Rain lowers pH (acidic water), dilutes alkalinity, dilutes calcium hardness, and may drop water temperature — all four LSI inputs move negative simultaneously; includes rain volume thresholds and post-rain correction order
- [How CYA Changes Your LSI Calculation](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/blog/cya-effect-on-lsi): CYA lowers effective alkalinity in the LSI formula via effective TA = TA − CYA/3; at CYA 80 the correction shifts LSI by ~0.15; indoor pools (no CYA) are unaffected; covers who it matters most for and how to compensate
- [Pool Calcium Hardness](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/blog/calcium-hardness-in-pools): Target ranges by pool type (plaster 200–400 ppm, vinyl 150–250 ppm), how to raise with calcium chloride, why no chemical can lower it (partial drain only), and why calcium is the biggest LSI lever
- [How to Lower Calcium Hardness](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/blog/how-to-lower-calcium-hardness): Partial drain and refill is the only method; dilution formula: drain% = (current − target) / (current − fill water CH); sequestering agents prevent scale deposition but do not lower CH; includes drain percentage examples and pool-type safety considerations
- [Pool Scale and Calcium Deposits](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/blog/pool-scale-calcium-deposits): What causes calcium carbonate scale (positive LSI), where it forms (tile line, heater, SWG cell), how to remove it (pumice, descaler, acid wash), how to descale a salt cell, and why it comes back if LSI isn't fixed
- [White Flakes from Pool Returns](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/blog/white-flakes-from-pool-returns): White flakes from return jets are usually calcium carbonate scale breaking loose from inside pipes or the heater — caused by positive LSI. How to use the acid test to confirm, how to fix the water chemistry, and how to distinguish from white water mold or filter media blowback
- [Scale Inside a Salt Cell](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/blog/salt-cell-calcium-scale): Calcium scale on SWG electrode plates caused by localized high-pH from electrolysis byproducts; how to clean with diluted muriatic acid (1:4, 15–20 min soak); what damages the ruthenium oxide coating; cleaning frequency as a diagnostic for LSI control; root-cause fix via pH and calcium management
- [Corrosive Pool Water](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/blog/corrosive-pool-water): Negative LSI causes — low CH, low pH, low TA, cold water; warning signs (etched plaster, blue-green copper staining, grout dissolution, heater failure); fix order (TA → pH → calcium hardness); special cases (spring opening, soft fill water, fresh plaster, repeated acid additions)
- [LSI in Saltwater Pools: Why SWG Owners Must Watch Balance](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/blog/lsi-saltwater-pools): Why SWG electrolysis constantly raises pH (NaOH byproduct), how this drives positive LSI, the TDS factor (salt slightly lowers LSI), why the salt cell accumulates scale faster than bulk LSI predicts, SWG-specific targets (pH 7.4–7.6, TA 60–80 ppm, CYA 70–80 ppm), managing acid additions proactively
- [Free Chlorine vs Total Chlorine: What's the Difference?](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/blog/free-chlorine-vs-total-chlorine): FC is active sanitizer, TC includes FC + combined chlorine (CC); CC = TC − FC; above 0.5 ppm CC shock is needed; covers ppm meaning, DPD/FAS-DPD/strip test methods, OTO kit warning, FC-low-but-TC-fine misreading, and breakpoint chlorination
- [What Causes High Combined Chlorine](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/blog/what-causes-high-combined-chlorine): Chloramines from bather waste, organic debris, low FC, rain, cloudy weather, or weak circulation; fix is breakpoint chlorination at roughly 10x current CC
- [Liquid Chlorine vs Tablets](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/blog/liquid-chlorine-vs-tablets): Liquid (sodium hypochlorite) doesn't raise CYA; tablets (trichlor) add CYA every dose and cause stabilizer lock — pick based on existing CYA level
- [How to Shock a Pool](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/blog/how-to-shock-a-pool): Shock target = CYA × 40% (breakpoint chlorination); add liquid chlorine at dusk, hold FC at shock target (retest every 4–6h), done when CC < 0.5 ppm + water clear + overnight FC loss ≤ 1 ppm
- [How Long After Shocking Can You Swim](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/blog/how-long-after-shocking-can-you-swim): No fixed wait time — swim when FC is back in the normal target range for your CYA; at CYA 50 that's below 7 ppm; always test before swimming
- [Why Does My Pool Smell Like Chlorine](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/blog/why-does-my-pool-smell-like-chlorine): Strong chlorine smell = combined chlorine (chloramines), not excess FC; properly maintained pools have almost no odor; fix is shock to breakpoint
- [Chlorine Lock Myth](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/blog/chlorine-lock-myth): Chlorine lock is not real chemistry; symptoms attributed to it are actually high CYA (requiring impractically high shock dose), active organic demand (algae consuming FC faster than added), or pH too high
- [Pool Chlorine Too High](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/blog/pool-chlorine-too-high): High FC after shock = expected, just wait; genuinely excessive FC: leave cover off for sunlight, dilute, or use sodium thiosulfate as last resort (dose carefully to avoid removing all FC)
- [Test Strips vs Liquid Test Kits](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/blog/test-strips-vs-liquid-test-kits): Strips are fast but imprecise (±20-30%); FAS-DPD drop kits (Taylor K-2006) are the standard for accurate FC readings; digital testers are a middle option — more accurate than strips but don't replace liquid kits for CYA
- [Baking Soda vs Soda Ash](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/blog/baking-soda-vs-soda-ash): Baking soda raises alkalinity, soda ash raises pH — using the wrong one for low pH makes chemistry worse
- [Pool Alkalinity vs pH](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/blog/pool-alkalinity-vs-ph): pH is acidity right now (target 7.4–7.8), TA is the buffer that keeps pH stable (target 60–120 ppm); fix TA first when both are off, drifting pH usually means TA is out of range
- [Pool pH Keeps Rising](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/blog/pool-ph-keeps-rising): Persistent pH drift is almost always high TA (>120), salt cell electrolysis, aeration features, fresh plaster cure, repeated cal-hypo/soda ash, or high daily liquid chlorine on low CYA — diagnostic-first instead of dosing forever
- [Saltwater vs Chlorine Pools](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/blog/saltwater-vs-chlorine-pools): SWG pools still use chlorine (generated from salt) — cost, maintenance, and chemistry differences vs traditional chlorine pools
- [How to Open Your Pool for Summer: Complete Step-by-Step Guide](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/blog/opening-pool-for-summer): Spring opening guide — uncover, top off, equipment check, test, balance, then shock; what to do in what order
- [How to Close a Pool for Winter: Step-by-Step Checklist](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/blog/how-to-close-a-pool-for-winter): Pool winterizing guide — when to close (water temp below 60°F), chemistry targets at closing (pH 7.4–7.8, TA 60–90, CH per surface type, CYA 30–50), shock dose (CYA × 40% min 10 ppm), algaecide timing (24–48h after shock below 5 ppm FC), water level adjustment by cover type, blowing out lines and plugging returns, draining pump/filter/heater/salt cell, cover installation; saltwater pool closing specifics; common mistakes
- [Pool Startup Chemicals Checklist](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/blog/pool-startup-chemicals-checklist): The 6 chemicals you need on hand for a fresh fill or seasonal opening, with dose estimates by pool size and above-ground notes
- [Pool Chemistry During a Heat Wave](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/blog/pool-chemistry-heat-wave): Heat accelerates FC consumption, shifts LSI positive (+0.08–0.10 per 10°F rise), and creates peak algae conditions; test FC daily, target upper FC range, lower pH slightly to counteract temperature-driven LSI rise
- [How to Test Pool Water at Home](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/blog/how-to-test-pool-water-at-home): Sampling technique (elbow-deep, away from returns), what each test measures, and how to read results without misinterpreting them
- [Why Track Pool Chemistry Over Time](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/blog/why-track-pool-chemistry-over-time): Single tests answer "what now," trend data answers "why" — chlorine demand, pH drift triggers, slow CYA climb, equipment aging, and seasonal drift only visible across many readings
- [How to Track Pool Chemicals (Simple System)](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/blog/how-to-track-pool-chemicals): The 4-step loop — test, record, dose, retest — with what to log (date + FC/pH/TA/CYA/CH + dose + one-line note), how often to log, and how to pick notebook vs spreadsheet vs phone app
- [Does High Alkalinity Cause Cloudy Pool Water?](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/blog/high-alkalinity-cloudy-pool): How high TA pushes pH up and causes calcium carbonate to precipitate as white haze; diagnosis, fix, and clearing timeline
- [Pool Cloudy After Shocking](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/blog/pool-cloudy-after-shocking): Why your pool is still cloudy after shocking and how to fix it
- [Does Liquid Chlorine Raise CYA? The Full Breakdown](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/blog/does-liquid-chlorine-raise-cya): Liquid chlorine adds zero CYA; trichlor tablets add ~0.6 ppm CYA per 1 ppm FC raised; full breakdown by chlorine type
- [How to Clear a Cloudy Pool Fast](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/blog/how-to-clear-cloudy-pool-fast): 5-step 24-hour plan: balance pH, shock to CYA level, brush, clean filter, run pump 24/7
- [Dead Algae But Pool Still Cloudy? Clear It in 1–3 Days](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/blog/dead-algae-still-cloudy): Confirm algae is dead with OCLT first; run pump 24/7, clean filter every 8–12 hours; clarifier for light haze, flocculant (vacuum to waste) as last resort; declare done when CC ≤ 0.5 ppm and OCLT passes
- [Pool Turned Green Overnight](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/blog/pool-turned-green-overnight): Fresh algae bloom from chlorine dropping below CYA minimum — triage in 5 minutes, then hold FC at shock level to clear in 3–7 days
- [Why Won't Chlorine Stay in My Pool](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/blog/why-wont-chlorine-stay-in-pool): 7 most common causes of chlorine loss — low CYA, high CYA, algae, organics, chloramines, underdosing, heat
- [Ideal Pool pH Level](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/blog/ideal-pool-ph-level): Ideal pool pH is 7.4–7.8 (7.5–7.6 sweet spot) — why pH matters, how to raise it (soda ash) and lower it (muriatic acid), with dose chart by pool size
- [How Much Muriatic Acid to Add to a Pool](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/blog/how-much-muriatic-acid-to-add-to-pool): Dose chart by pool size for lowering pH or alkalinity; includes 31.45% vs 14.5% strengths, safety, step-by-step

- [Desert Pool Chemistry: The Complete Guide](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/blog/desert-pool-chemistry): Why desert pools in Arizona, Southern California, and Nevada need higher CYA (60–80 ppm), higher FC targets (CYA × 7.5% + climate buffer), and active calcium management — high evaporation, hard fill water, intense UV, and year-round heat all require different targets than national guides recommend
- [Pool Evaporation in Hot Climates](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/blog/pool-evaporation-hot-climates): Desert pools lose 1–1.5 inches/week in summer vs. 0.25–0.5 for temperate climates; every evaporated gallon concentrates minerals left behind; bucket test to measure your pool's rate; solar cover reduces evaporation 75–90%; fall partial drain resets accumulated calcium and CYA
- [Year-Round Pool Maintenance for Desert Pools](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/blog/year-round-pool-maintenance-desert-pools): No winterizing, no spring startup shock, no annual chemistry reset for AZ/SoCal/NV pools; seasonal calendar (spring CYA/CH check, summer daily FC + monthly LSI, fall partial drain, winter LSI flip toward corrosive); calcium hardness, CYA, and TDS accumulate year over year without planned drains
- [Calcium Creep Explained](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/blog/calcium-creep-explained): How evaporation concentrates minerals (pure water leaves, dissolved calcium stays) + hard fill water adds 7–10 ppm CH per week; 15,000-gal pool at 300 ppm fill water gains ~168 ppm CH over a 24-week desert summer; targets: 200–400 ppm (OK), 400–500 (elevated, manage pH), 500–600 (plan drain), 600+ (drain/RO now); temperature shifts LSI +0.25 from spring to summer peak alone
- [Why Arizona Pools Have High Calcium Hardness](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/blog/why-arizona-pools-have-high-calcium): Phoenix tap water 200–320 ppm CH (SRP/CAP blend); Scottsdale 230–350 ppm (higher CAP); Tucson 200–300 ppm; Las Vegas 280–380 ppm; inland SoCal similar via Colorado River; fill water at or above pool target range means no dilution effect — every top-off adds calcium; evaporation compounds it ~7 ppm/week; Consumer Confidence Report lists fill water hardness
- [When to Drain a Desert Pool](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/blog/when-to-drain-a-desert-pool): 4 triggers: CYA >80–100 ppm, CH >500–600 ppm, very high TDS, visible tile scale; best time: October–November (fall peak accumulation); 25–33% partial drain lowers all dissolved parameters proportionally (25% drain: CYA 90→67, CH 520→390); full drains rarely needed + structural risk; discharge to sanitary sewer (not storm drain); alternative: reverse osmosis
- [Reverse Osmosis vs. Draining a Pool](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/blog/reverse-osmosis-vs-draining-a-pool): Drain removes water proportionally (~25% reduction per parameter, refills with hard AZ tap); RO removes minerals without losing water (membrane rejects Ca, CYA, TDS); RO cost $400–900 vs drain $30–80 + chemicals; RO starting point: near-zero CH rebalanced to 250 ppm; drain starting point: already 390 ppm CH with hard fill water; RO preferred for salt pools (preserves salt investment), water-scarce areas, very high TDS, pools never treated
- [How to Kill Pool Algae](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/blog/how-to-kill-pool-algae): Shock target = CYA × 40%; brush all surfaces daily to disrupt biofilm; run pump 24/7; hold FC at shock level until CC ≤ 0.5 ppm + water clear + OCLT passes; green algae 3–7 days; mustard algae needs algaecide + swimsuit decontamination; black algae needs wire brush + 1–2 weeks
- [Mustard Algae vs. Green Algae](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/blog/mustard-algae-vs-green-algae): Green algae clouds the water; mustard algae is yellow-brown slime in shaded spots that brushes off but keeps coming back; mustard algae is chlorine-resistant and survives on swimsuits and equipment — must wash all suits (hot wash + high heat dry) and decontaminate gear after treatment or it reappears immediately
- [Black Algae in a Pool](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/blog/black-algae-in-pool): Black algae is cyanobacteria, not true algae; forms polysaccharide shell that blocks chlorine; roots holdfasts into plaster and concrete (never in vinyl); treatment requires stainless-steel wire brushing before every chlorine dose + sustained shock-level FC for 1–2 weeks; optional: trichlor tablet rubbed directly on colony after brushing
- [Why Algae Keeps Coming Back](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/blog/algae-keeps-coming-back): 5 root causes — (1) FC below CYA minimum between tests, (2) CYA above 70–80 ppm making chlorine ineffective at normal doses, (3) shock treatment stopped before OCLT passed, (4) swimsuit/equipment recontamination (mustard algae), (5) circulation dead spots; tracking readings over time reveals which pattern applies
- [Pool Cloudy After Rain](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/blog/cloudy-pool-after-rain): Rain dilutes free chlorine (even 1 inch can drop FC 1–3 ppm in a typical pool), washes algae spores + phosphates from runoff into the water, and raises pool water level diluting all chemistry; test FC within hours of a storm; if FC is below minimum, add chlorine immediately; if green tint or FC near zero for 24+ hours, shock to CYA × 40%; rainwater is pH 5.0–5.6 (slightly acidic) and can lower pool pH
- [Pool Cloudy but Chemistry Fine — Filter Issue](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/blog/cloudy-pool-filter-not-working): When FC/pH/TA/CH all test in range but water stays cloudy, the problem is filtration not chemistry; 4 causes: (1) insufficient run time — need 8–12h/day for full turnover, (2) dirty/clogged filter — backwash sand/DE or clean cartridge, (3) worn-out media — sand >5–7 years, cartridge >1–2 seasons, (4) channeling in sand (water finds bypass paths through media); clarifier helps after filter is cleaned; broken laterals (sand in return jets) or cracked grids (DE in returns) require repair
- [Pool Cloudy After Adding Chemicals](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/blog/cloudy-pool-after-adding-chemicals): Brief cloudiness after granular chemicals is normal — CYA granules cloud 30–60 min while dissolving (add via skimmer); calcium chloride clouds 15–30 min (normal exothermic reaction); soda ash causes brief cloud at pour point (normal), persists if overdosed with high CH because pH spike precipitates calcium carbonate; baking soda minimal cloudiness unless TA overdose pushes pH up in hard water; clarifier can briefly increase visible haze as particles clump before filter catches them; liquid chlorine and muriatic acid cause no cloudiness; cloudiness >24 hours is calcium carbonate precipitation — test pH and correct to 7.4–7.6 then filter

## Explained (Pool Chemistry Reference)

- [Pool Chemistry Explained](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/explained/): Plain-language reference for every pool chemistry term — what each means, target ranges, why it matters
- [Free Chlorine](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/explained/free-chlorine): Free chlorine (FC) is the active sanitizer; target depends on CYA level, not a single fixed number
- [Total Chlorine](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/explained/total-chlorine): TC = FC + CC (chloramines); when TC equals FC, no chloramines are present; the number most test strips report
- [Combined Chlorine](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/explained/combined-chlorine): CC = TC − FC; chloramines that cause pool smell and eye irritation; target < 0.5 ppm; fix is breakpoint chlorination
- [Cyanuric Acid](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/explained/cyanuric-acid): CYA protects chlorine from UV; target 30–50 (60–80 for SWG); too much CYA causes most pool problems
- [FC/CYA Ratio](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/explained/fc-cya-ratio): FC must be at least CYA × 7.5% for standard pools (CYA × 5% for SWG); below this threshold chlorine stops killing algae effectively
- [Chloramines](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/explained/chloramines): Spent chlorine compounds from sweat/urine/oils that cause 'pool smell' and red eyes — fix is more chlorine, not less
- [Breakpoint Chlorination](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/explained/breakpoint-chlorination): The process of raising FC to shock level (CYA × 40%) to chemically destroy chloramines; must hold until CC < 0.5 ppm and FC holds overnight
- [Total Alkalinity](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/explained/total-alkalinity): TA buffers pH from swinging; target 60–120 ppm; high TA causes persistent pH drift upward, low TA causes erratic pH swings
- [pH](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/explained/ph): Measure of water acidity; target 7.4–7.8; affects chlorine effectiveness and swimmer comfort; fix TA first when both are off
- [Langelier Saturation Index (LSI)](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/explained/lsi): Single number indicating if water will corrode, scale, or stay balanced; target -0.3 to +0.3
- [Calcium Hardness](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/explained/calcium-hardness): Dissolved calcium in pool water; biggest single LSI lever; target 200–400 ppm plaster, 150–250 vinyl; only drain reduces it
- [Phosphates](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/explained/phosphates): Algae nutrient source in pool water; elevated phosphates increase chlorine demand and fuel algae blooms when FC slips
- [Salt](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/explained/salt): Sodium chloride dissolved at 2700–3400 ppm to power a salt water generator; SWG minimum FC = CYA × 5%; positive LSI deposits calcium scale on cell plates

## Pool Calculators

- [Pool Calculators](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/tools/): Free pool chemistry calculators — volume, chlorine dose, shock level, and more
- [Pool Volume Calculator](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/tools/pool-volume-calculator): Calculate pool gallons by shape (rectangle, oval, round, kidney, L-shape) with sloped depth, spa, and tanning shelf correction options
- [Chlorine Dose Calculator](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/tools/chlorine-dose-calculator): How much liquid chlorine or cal-hypo to add to raise FC to target; supports 10%, 12.5%, cal-hypo 65%/73%, and trichlor (with CYA warning)
- [Pool Shock Calculator](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/tools/pool-shock-calculator): Shock target FC = CYA × 40%; calculates how much chlorine needed to reach breakpoint chlorination level from current FC
- [Pool pH Calculator](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/tools/pool-ph-calculator): Raise or lower pool pH — muriatic acid (31.45% or 14.5%) to lower pH with TA correction for accuracy, or soda ash (sodium carbonate) to raise pH; target range 7.4–7.8
- [Muriatic Acid Calculator](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/tools/muriatic-acid-calculator): How much muriatic acid to lower pH (uses current pH, target pH, and TA for accuracy) or lower total alkalinity; supports 31.45% and 14.5% strengths
- [Baking Soda Calculator](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/tools/baking-soda-calculator): How much baking soda (sodium bicarbonate) to raise total alkalinity to target; dose in ounces and pounds; target TA 60–90 ppm
- [CYA Dilution Calculator](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/tools/cya-dilution-calculator): How many gallons to drain and refill to lower CYA to target; includes staged drain guidance when reduction requires draining more than 50% of the pool
- [LSI Calculator](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/tools/lsi-calculator): Calculate pool Langelier Saturation Index using the full formula — CYA-corrected alkalinity (TA minus CYA/3), polynomial temperature factor, salt TDS adjustment; shows per-factor breakdown so you can see what's driving your water balance score; target -0.3 to +0.3
- [Saltwater Pool Salt Calculator](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/tools/saltwater-pool-salt-calculator): How many pounds of pool salt (NaCl) to add to reach target salinity ppm for salt chlorine generator (SWG) pools; supports 40 lb and 50 lb bag sizes; typical SWG target 2700–3400 ppm
- [Calcium Hardness Calculator](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/tools/calcium-hardness-calculator): How much calcium chloride to raise pool calcium hardness (CH) to target; supports 77% CaCl2 flake and 96% anhydrous; target 250–350 ppm for plaster, 150–250 ppm for fiberglass/vinyl; CH affects LSI water balance score
- [Dry Acid to Muriatic Acid Calculator](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/tools/dry-acid-calculator): Convert between dry acid (sodium bisulfate, pH Down) and muriatic acid (hydrochloric acid) — bidirectional conversion based on equivalent hydrogen ions; supports 93.2% and 90% dry acid, 31.45% and 14.5% muriatic; includes quick reference table and sulfate buildup warning
- [Chlorine Cost Calculator](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/tools/chlorine-cost-calculator): Compare the true seasonal cost of liquid chlorine (12.5% sodium hypochlorite), trichlor tablets (90%), and cal-hypo (65%) — includes CYA drain cost from trichlor buildup (0.6 ppm CYA per ppm FC raised, drain when CYA hits 80 ppm, 62% partial drain to reset to 30 ppm); inputs: pool volume, current CYA, season length, weekly FC demand, local prices; outputs: cost/week, chemical cost/season, drain events, true season total with best-value badge
- [Pool Chlorine Usage Calculator](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/tools/pool-chlorine-usage-calculator): Operational weekly chlorine usage and monthly cost — inputs: pool volume, chlorine product (liquid 10%, liquid 12.5%, or cal-hypo 65%), price per gallon/lb, demand level (preset: Low 1 ppm/day, Moderate 2.5, High 5, Very High 8; or custom ppm/day), optional demand measurement from two FC readings + hours between (auto-fills demand field), optional season length in weeks; outputs: daily dose (fl oz or gal/lbs), weekly quantity with container equivalents (1-gal/2.5-gal jugs or 5-lb/25-lb buckets), weekly cost, monthly cost, season total cost; demand constants: LIQUID10 = 0.001190 fl oz/ppm/gal, LIQUID125 = 0.000952 fl oz/ppm/gal, CAL-HYPO = 1/7.8 lbs/ppm/10k gal
- [Pool Opening Calculator](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/tools/pool-opening-calculator): Spring opening chemical shopping list — inputs: pool volume, surface type (plaster/gunite vs vinyl/fiberglass), pool condition (clear/covered, cloudy, green/algae), SWG toggle, optional FC/pH/TA/CYA/CH; outputs: numbered shopping list in correct addition order (CYA stabilizer first if CYA < target → baking soda → pH → calcium chloride → shock → algaecide); shock dose scales by condition (clear: CYA × 40% min 10 ppm, cloudy: 1.5× min 20 ppm, green/algae: 3× min 30 ppm) using 65% cal-hypo; CYA step gated before shock when CYA < 30 ppm (< 60 for SWG) with 24–48h dissolve wait note; algaecide is required step for green pools, optional for clear/cloudy; optional metal sequestrant for iron/copper in fill water; warnings for high CYA (drain required) and high CH; all chemistry inputs optional — works as a pre-test shopping estimate when only volume and condition are known
- [Pool Closing Calculator](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/tools/pool-closing-calculator): Winterizing chemical shopping list based on pool size and current readings — inputs: pool volume, surface type (plaster/gunite vs vinyl/fiberglass), optional FC/pH/TA/CYA/CH; outputs: numbered shopping list in correct addition order (baking soda → pH → calcium chloride → shock → algaecide); shock dose = CYA × 40% min 10 ppm with 65% cal-hypo; CH target accounts for calcium added by shock; warnings for high CYA (>70 ppm, plan partial drain at opening) and high CH; optional enzyme treatment
- [Overnight Chlorine Loss Test (OCLT) Calculator](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/tools/overnight-chlorine-loss-test): Pass/fail verdict for the overnight chlorine loss test — inputs: FC at dusk and FC at dawn (required); optional CYA, pool volume, and chlorine product (10%/12.5%) for a shock dose on failure; verdict thresholds: pass ≤1 ppm loss, borderline 1–2 ppm (retest recommended), fail >2 ppm (active organic demand); special cases for FC hitting 0 overnight (invalid/fail) and morning FC higher than evening (testing error); fail path shows shock target (CYA × 40%), FC to add, and fl oz dose; next-steps card for each verdict outcome
- [Chemical Addition Order Calculator](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/tools/pool-chemical-addition-order): Step-by-step treatment plan when multiple parameters are out of range — inputs: pool volume, surface type (plaster/vinyl), SWG toggle, FC, TC, pH, TA, CH, CYA; outputs: prioritized numbered step cards with chemical name, exact dose, and wait time between steps; shopping list summary; correct sequencing (TA → pH → CYA → CH → FC/shock); handles pH/TA interaction cases (aerate-first when pH is low and TA is high; acid-aerate cycle when both are high); drain notes for parameters that cannot be chemically adjusted (high CYA, high CH)
- [Water Replacement Calculator](https://www.poolchemtracker.com/tools/water-replacement-calculator): Multi-parameter pool dilution calculator — inputs: pool volume, surface type (plaster/vinyl), current and target values for CYA, calcium hardness (with optional fill water CH for hard-water corrections), salt, copper, and nitrates; outputs: recommended drain percentage (controlled by the most-demanding parameter), gallons to drain, and per-parameter projected values after the recommended drain; staged drain guidance when drain exceeds 50%; can't-fix warning when fill water CH is at or above target CH (reverse osmosis recommended instead)
